sources.originalTitle: 5 $1M+ AI startup ideas from an indie hacker legend
sources.summary: Danny Postma explains how he finds low-competition keywords in Ahrefs and fills pages with AI-generated content. He also covers why AI products should feel like the human service they replace, and why boring niche verticals have little competition. He argues the window is short, so speed matters.

principles.text: Find keywords with real search intent and near-zero difficulty, then use AI to generate the content at scale.
principles.quote: basically figure out where there's a lot of search intent and very low keyword difficulty

principles.text: Let users generate content with your AI tool and publish it on your site, so the site grows itself.
principles.quote: it's basically user generated content using AI to fill your website and within a month you're probably going to generate like hundreds of thousands of pieces of content Google's going to love it

principles.text: Early movers in SEO keep their lead, so the window for AI niches is short and speed matters.
principles.quote: the first to market the first to build the backlinks the first to get their like the domain names and stuff they will mostly stay on the top of the market in that sense

principles.text: Make AI feel like the human service it replaces; mainstream users adopt products that feel familiar.
principles.quote: if you want to get products to be adopted you need to make it feel like the real world

principles.text: Boring, unglamorous industries have little competition, so a vertical AI tool can own the whole market.
principles.quote: no one is going to make an AI app for a doctor or whatever there's no there's no competition in it because it's boring

principles.text: Seed a marketplace by listing the most requested jobs from an existing platform, as Airbnb did on Craigslist.
principles.quote: you can just seat your platform in that way

sources.title: Danny Postma on AI products as marketing, SEO-first launches, and staying a small bootstrapped builder
sources.originalTitle: From Zero to Millions: Danny Postma Reveals AI App Strategies for Success
sources.summary: Danny explains how he ships fast AI mini products (This Model Does Not Exist, ProfilePicture.AI, Tattoos.AI) and uses them as marketing for his main product. He covers why he sold Headlime instead of scaling a team, why bigger competitors help him, and why SEO plus tools, not blog posts, is the durable way to launch.

principles.text: Launch small side products as a marketing channel for your main product, rather than relying on ads.
principles.quote: what I like to do is I like to create products like launch mini products as a marketing

principles.text: Pick your path deliberately: Danny sold Headlime rather than raise and manage a 50-person team, because that life would not make him happy.
principles.quote: I knew like it wouldn't be my life to work 80 hours manage people that's not it's not going to make me happy so I'm going to do that so I decided to sell it

principles.text: Larger funded competitors can help a small bootstrapper: they spend on awareness and you capture the spillover search traffic.
principles.quote: it's only good if a competitor built something like you because they have the money to create awareness

principles.text: Stay small on purpose: don't chase huge scale if it forces you to build a big team and support load.
principles.quote: if I get millions of customers like how am I going to handle the whole support load and everything it means I have to hire a whole team

principles.text: Know your weakness: he starts and explores products, then hires people to run operations and build out the boring features.
principles.quote: I build out the products I'm exploring it I'm launching new ideas and he is hired to build out once I let's say bluntly once I get bored of it

principles.text: For a first product, find keywords with low difficulty in Ahrefs, build a product around them, and rank with SEO.
principles.quote: keep on typing in keywords of things that you might be interested in until you find a collection of keywords that has a keyword difficulty under 10

sources.title: Danny Postma: Demand-first SEO product picking, one-off B2C payments, and moving from solo to team
sources.originalTitle: Danny Postma — An Indie Hacker's Business Evolution
sources.summary: Danny explains how he picks products by searching Ahrefs for high-search, low-difficulty keywords so he never has to market, why he favors one-off B2C payments over SaaS, how he handles copycats, and why he's now hiring a remote async team at 29 to run his portfolio like a studio.

principles.text: Only build products where search demand exists and keyword difficulty is low; Google then replaces marketing.
principles.quote: the easiest thing you can do is pick a product that has a lot of searches with no competition you never have to do marketing because you're going to rank number one on Google

principles.text: Keyword difficulty under roughly 10-20 plus a couple of backlinks all but guarantees front-page ranking.
principles.quote: the moment you have like a keyword difficulty that's under 10 or 20 you're guaranteed to go to the front page if you have like a one or two backlinks

principles.text: Don't try to create a market as an indie hacker; find existing demand and compute potential revenue from conversion rate and rank.
principles.quote: if no one searches in it for Google it means you have to create the market

principles.text: One-off B2C purchases mean little support, no feature treadmill, and growth via SEO, ads and conversion optimization.
principles.quote: you only have to get them ones to buy there's no recurring thing you don't have to add features because they don't pay monthly

principles.text: Automate support and refunds so products run without you being online; avoid tools that depend on you always being there.
principles.quote: I don't build tools and software that really rely on me always being there

principles.text: Buy underperforming traffic assets and fix conversion: a better landing page multiplies revenue and pays back the price fast.
principles.quote: if I can optimize the landing page to have five times more conversions I run back the equation price in 10 months

sources.title: How Danny Postma built Headlime on GPT-3 in 8 months and sold it to Jasper for seven figures
sources.originalTitle: Danny Postma: OpenAI, GPT-3, AI Business Ideas & His 7-Figure Sale
sources.summary: Danny Postma explains how he taught himself to code, scratched his own itch with a string of products, and built Headlime on GPT-3 until Jasper acquired it. He also covers where AI products win (marketing, UI, private models) and why he sold instead of raising or hiring.

principles.text: Build products that scratch your own itch, so even with zero buyers you still have a tool you use.
principles.quote: I think it's mostly scratching my own itch because then it's fun to work on it because it solves actual problem. So, if no one buys it, I literally use it.

principles.text: Ship fast and expect many misses: Headlime was product three, ProfilePicture.ai was product eleven.
principles.quote: So, I got lucky with Headline to be number product number three to be successful. Yeah. But, now with Profile Picture, I took 11 products to get there.

principles.text: Share wins, losses and revenue publicly on Twitter; building in public doubles as your marketing channel.
principles.quote: I kept sharing all my wins, my losses, my revenue gains, my learnings and basically I I I started growing my followers while building Headlime on Twitter while Indie Hacking, which is a really good marketing way.

principles.text: In a crowded AI wrapper space, the moat is marketing, a good interface, and privately trained models, not the API.
principles.quote: there's hundreds like when I launched Headline, there were 50 other people doing the exact same things. And it's all comes down to are you good at marketing and do you have a good graphical user interface? Those are I think the most important things to have now in AI or the third one is privately trained models.

principles.text: Learn to code by building a real project and solving each blocker as it appears, using free YouTube tutorials.
principles.quote: if you start a little project, you you will hit those little barriers, figure out how to solve those little barriers and go to the top.

principles.text: Start no-code for 0 to 1, then move to code and self-hosting for control once it scales.
principles.quote: If you want to have full control over it, coding is always the best way to go cuz you can absolutely customize it 100% and you're not susceptible to the platform where you build it on

principles.text: Distribution and marketing matter more than building, especially in AI where wrappers have little moat.
principles.quote: you got to do distribution is everything marketing is everything it's really important it's always been important with product launches and especially with AI where you have less of a modes

principles.quote: focus on like something small some small problems to solve and do your marketing to the distribution don't just build you got to sell it

principles.quote: profile picture was just dream move it was there was no mode on it and what I'm doing with head Shield is basically it's 15 different AI models stacked on top of each other

sources.title: How Danny Postma used lifetime deals, scarcity and open building to sell Headlime, and what copycats taught him
sources.originalTitle: Bruno Talks With Danny Postma • Building in public, pros and cons
sources.summary: Danny Postma explains how he launched Headlime with tiered, scarcity-limited lifetime deals, listened to early customers to decide features, and grew via building in public. He also covers the downside: his easily copied product was cloned about 10 times, and he now advises caution with revenue numbers.

principles.text: Lifetime deals give early cash runway and recruit enthusiastic early adopters; treat them like a small angel investment from customers.
principles.quote: it feels like a small angel investment for my customers um in that way that i have a year now of money to work on this project

principles.text: Use tiered lifetime pricing to discover willingness to pay: sell out a cheap tier, then raise the price and repeat.
principles.quote: i think it's a really good way also to validate what is the price people want to pay for you to

principles.text: Build a feature once three customers ask for it; one request is too weak a signal.
principles.quote: if three people ask me for a feature i build it if one person asks you for a feature it's it's like a small chance that they will even use it

principles.text: Ask why customers want a feature before building it, since the request may not match the real need.
principles.quote: customers say one thing they probably mean something else so try to elaborate on it try to learn what they really really want ask for examples for it

principles.text: Use real scarcity to create urgency, and never fake it, because it destroys trust.
principles.quote: don't mess with those tactics don't fake it like booking.com with the last rooms

principles.text: Sell a tool by showing it saves customers more money or time than it costs, and keep shipping fast and openly.
principles.quote: if they use this tool and it saves them already one hour of their working time they already earned it back

sources.title: How Danny Postma built AgentOS on Claude's Agent SDK to automate 95% of his work
sources.originalTitle: How I Built My Own AgentOS on Claude's Agent SDK (So You Can Too)
sources.summary: Danny walks through the autonomous agent system he built over six months on Claude managed agents. It runs tasks, triggers, cron automations and open-ended goal loops in isolated containers, and only pings him via an inbox when stuck. The video covers agent permission walling, template-driven dev workflows, spend caps and cost control.

principles.text: Stop babysitting a terminal; use cron jobs and triggers so agents run for hours and you return to finished work.
principles.quote: you want to overload things, come back 4 hours later and it's done. I want to have cron jobs. I want to have triggers that start the tasks.

principles.text: Give each agent only the access it needs, so a leak or prompt injection has nothing to exploit.
principles.quote: you don't want to give any access to your agent that they don't need.

principles.text: Run every agent session in a fresh disposable container that pulls the repo, does the task, commits, then is thrown away.
principles.quote: after every session, this container is thrown away and the next session has to reinitialize the whole project again cleanly

principles.text: Agents message you only when they need you; you don't manage or wait on them.
principles.quote: whenever they need me and only whenever they need me, they will send me a message in my inbox.

principles.text: Build multi-step workflows as templates with human approval gates and separate review agents, since the plan isn't trusted by default.
principles.quote: I don't trust the plan by itself, so I want a review coordinator to spin up four different review agents

principles.text: For open-ended work, run goal loops against a definition of done, with a spend cap, time limit and stuck limit.
principles.quote: every definition done has a limitation, so it has a spend cap cuz I run one goal without spend cap one one night and it direct up to $1,000

sources.title: How Danny built a free "explore design" skill to stop AI making ugly landing pages
sources.originalTitle: How I Stopped AI From Designing Ugly Landing Pages (Free Skill)
sources.summary: Danny explains a free AI skill that fixes sloppy, generic AI landing pages. It scans your brand once, explores several hero or section designs with trade-offs, lets you combine options, then implements the winner. He runs it section by section because AI can't hold a whole page in context.

principles.text: Scan brand (colors, typography, style) once, then reuse it so AI designs stay consistent.
principles.quote: it invokes first a brand scan. It's going to take a look at what is your color systems, what is your typography, what is the design style that you have. And this only runs once.

principles.text: Have AI explore several distinct design directions with trade-offs, then choose, instead of accepting one output.
principles.quote: it gives you four options. Basically, with its own trade-offs, what's the risk, and what happens if you pick this.

principles.text: Combine the best parts of two options into a new hybrid rather than settling for one.
principles.quote: you can tell the skill to basically, okay, make a version that combines this one and A into an option E.

principles.text: Prioritize a clear call to action and a visual showing what the product does.
principles.quote: this one has a clear place to stop the the the generator. It has the visuals on the right side.

principles.text: Design a landing page section by section, since AI can't hold the whole page in context.
principles.quote: you want to run this for every section of your landing page because you cannot do this for the whole website cuz the AI doesn't have the context to hold the whole context

principles.text: Distribute tools free on your own site to build goodwill and reach.
principles.quote: it's free on my website. I've published it for free. You can go to danny.md, click the explore design file

sources.title: How Danny Postma built and sold Headlime for 7 figures in 8 months
sources.originalTitle: Building & Selling a SaaS for +$1M in 8 Months (Failory interview with Danny Postma)
sources.summary: Danny explains how he turned an old headline-formulas book into a tool, launched with a lifetime deal, then pivoted to GPT-3 and grew from $1K to $20K MRR in public before selling to Jarvis.ai. Lessons on building for yourself, shipping fast, and building in public.

principles.text: Build something you'd use yourself; you are the most knowledgeable customer and it's worth something even if no one buys it.
principles.quote: Make something you'd like to use yourself. Even if no one buys it, it's still worth something to you. Furthermore, you are the most knowledgeable customer and know exactly what you want.

principles.text: Pick ideas that are easy to build and quick to validate, before wasting years on them.
principles.quote: Ideas that would be easy to build and validate before wasting years on them.

principles.text: Turn content you already own into a tool: tools are worth more than books.
principles.quote: 1) books are worth less than tools, and 2) it would be easy for me to build it, as I already had all the content ready.

principles.text: A limited one-time-fee deal can power a launch: over $60K in sales in the first few weeks.
principles.quote: The launch was an instant success, with over $60,000 in sales in the first few weeks. Most of this was thanks to a limited deal I launched, which gave customers access for a one-time fee instead of paying a subscription fee.

principles.text: Listen to customer feedback and ship fast; customers wanted far more than he first imagined.
principles.quote: Customers did not only want headline templates. They wanted all types of content, like emails, Facebook Headlines, and Google Ads.

principles.text: Build in public: a product won't market itself, so share what you're working on.
principles.quote: A product won’t market itself. And a great and easy way to do so is by just sharing what amazing stuff you’re working on.

sources.title: How Danny Postma pivoted from Stock AI to HeadshotPro and built a team
sources.originalTitle: Danny Postma, Founder of HeadshotPro (Unite.AI interview)
sources.summary: Danny Postma traces his path from Landingfolio and Headlime to HeadshotPro, showing how he pivoted fast when the market spoke. He covers shipping in 30 hours, differentiating on quality and focus, and overcoming his fear of hiring.

principles.text: Stay flexible and pivot based on what the market tells you, not on press attention.
principles.quote: While Deep Agency garnered a lot of press attention, it didn't translate into sales. On the other hand, HeadshotPro was an instant hit.

principles.text: Ship fast when a new technology window opens; beating a competitor to market matters.
principles.quote: I quickly developed and launched my product within 30 hours, beating a competitor to market.

principles.text: Differentiate by obsessing over output quality, not by relying on the same open-source models as everyone else.
principles.quote: Photo quality is our primary differentiator from other AI headshot generators.

principles.text: Stay focused on one niche instead of drifting horizontally into adjacent products.
principles.quote: Our sole focus is creating the highest quality, professional AI headshots.

principles.text: Improve a little every day; small daily iterations compound toward an ambitious quality goal.
principles.quote: If the model improves by 1% each day, there's no reason why we can't reach that goal, or get really close to it, by the end of this year.

principles.text: Hire earlier than feels comfortable; a team does things a solo founder can't and makes the work less lonely.
principles.quote: Looking back, I should have started a team way earlier.

sources.title: How Danny Postma launched, cloned-proofed and monetized AI products (Headlime, Profile Picture AI)
sources.originalTitle: Yo! Podcast 015: Danny Postma with Rob Hope on AI trends, lifetime deals, domains and landing pages
sources.summary: Danny Postma explains how he sold Headlime for seven figures, made $50K in two weeks with Profile Picture AI, and what he learned about clones, lifetime deals, domains, landing pages and building on API infrastructure. Core lessons: ship in public, differentiate on marketing and UI, validate with one-time payments, and use existing infrastructure for speed.

principles.text: Ship in public immediately; clones come anyway, and a product nobody knows about gets no traction.
principles.quote: if we didn't ship it in public like no one knew about the products. And how are you gonna. If you're. If you're too scared that people clone your product, you're never going to take off.

principles.text: When everyone uses the same AI tech, differentiate through marketing and a crisp UI.
principles.quote: if everyone's using the same tools, yeah, you need to market it and you need to have a nice tool because you're only differentiating are both those two.

principles.text: Validate an idea with a one-time/lifetime payment, then add subscriptions once you know what customers want.
principles.quote: if you want to validate an idea, make it a one time payment.

principles.text: Pay more for API providers instead of self-hosting; the time saved is worth far more than the cost.
principles.quote: you pay five times more for the A for the API. But you save 2 to 3 weeks of your time while someone else could have launched.

principles.text: Build by listening to customers rather than coding in secret; the final product comes from user feedback.
principles.quote: the only way you know what to build is by listening to customers.

principles.text: Landing pages: strong copy beats design; keep one CTA, show the product, and use Cialdini-style influence like scarcity and social proof.
principles.quote: You can just make a blank page, have a photo in the header, a title, a subtitle, and a call to action. That's enough.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny Postma explains how he finds low-competition keywords in Ahrefs and fills pages with AI-generated content. He also covers why AI products should feel like the human service they replace, and why boring niche verticals have little competition. He argues the window is short, so speed matters.

chunks.heading: AI plus SEO keyword generator sites
chunks.text:
- Danny's core tactic: pair AI content generation with low-competition search keywords. He logs into Ahrefs, types in a seed keyword and looks for high search intent with very low keyword difficulty. Ahrefs scores difficulty 0-100; near 0 means little competition and you can rank quickly.
- The old bottleneck was producing the content. He cites his own inspiration gallery, Landingfolio, where ranking was quick but content creation took a lot of time. AI removes that bottleneck: "you can just rapid fire and let things generate."
- Worked example, AI tattoos: searching "tattoos" in Ahrefs returns thousands of long-tail keywords (butterfly tattoo, dragon tattoo, bird tattoo). Generate images for each with Stable Diffusion, Midjourney or whatever is current, and fill directory pages (for example a page of butterfly tattoos).
- The loop: build a tool users pay to use, then show their generated output on the site as user-generated content. This feeds the directories organically. He says you can generate "hundreds of thousands of pieces of content" in a month, Google rewards it, and traffic follows.
- His result: the AI tattoo site reached about $10,000 MRR before he sold it to focus on another startup.
- He says it works for anything AI-related combined with low-difficulty content.
- Possible upsell: a lower-ticket product (tool access) plus a higher-ticket done-for-you service. Entrepreneurs who want to build these sites are high-value customers who need tools and services.

chunks.heading: Timing and the window of opportunity
chunks.text:
- Danny compares this to the early Apple App Store, when you could make money with a flashlight, calculator or fart app: "the golden age of AI and SEO combined."
- He expects it to stop working within about two years, because the niches will be found and filled by highly automated players.
- With SEO, he believes the first to market, first to build backlinks and first to claim the domains mostly stay on top.
- His own experience at Headshot Pro: when it started there were three or four competitors, then AI boilerplates led to roughly 1,000. He says Headshot Pro got lucky to be in the top three, and "the top three will always win."
- His advice: you can still compete in a busy market, but you must be fast. In AI tools, coming in a year later is probably too late. Find niches in Ahrefs with keyword difficulty of 0-5 before they are taken.

chunks.heading: ComfyUI template marketplace
chunks.text:
- ComfyUI is a drag-and-drop node interface for building visual AI pipelines (inputs, data processing, outputs). Previously anything deeper than calling ChatGPT meant writing Python.
- Danny is rebuilding his own Python workflows in ComfyUI because it is easier, and it can now run in the cloud (he mentions Replicate).
- The idea: YouTubers already publish ComfyUI workflow tutorials. Instead, build a marketplace where people sell, rent out or charge fees for exported workflow templates. He expects ComfyUI adoption to boom within months, and compares it to Indie Hackers who sell code boilerplates.
- He says this is the idea he would build himself if he weren't busy, and he shared it publicly so it exists.
- He is open to partnering: he told listeners with the skills to DM him on Twitter.

chunks.heading: Partnering as an audience owner
chunks.text:
- Danny is conscious of being too busy to take on more ideas while still working full-time on his company with a team.
- His view: if you have an audience, partnering with builders is an option. He notes you should offer more than an audience.
- Key tension he names: supporting another business costs free time after years of heavy work, so he weighs that sacrifice before partnering.
- He recalls that Greg's push 1.5 years earlier led him to start an AI influencer project that turned into Headshot Pro.

chunks.heading: Fiverr/Upwork 2.0: hire AI workers instead of freelancers
chunks.text:
- Concept: a clone of Fiverr or Upwork where you hire AI workflows (LLM-based bots) that feel like hiring a person. Danny doesn't know of anyone who has built this.
- Example: a translation job. Instead of finding a freelancer to translate an Excel sheet, the customer drops in the file and gets it back translated a day later, fully automated by AI.
- Why it works: normal people are afraid of AI or can't build APIs, so packaging it as a job marketplace is easier to sell. Customers don't want to babysit or fact-check; they dump the task and get the output.
- Supply side: let a community build workflows (possibly on ComfyUI) and offer them as services. The platform takes about a 5% fee; a builder might charge, for example, one cent per row.
- Getting customers: list the service on Upwork itself, and look at the most requested jobs on Upwork to decide what to automate. He mentions a known workaround for Upwork's anti-scraper blacklist. He compares seeding to Airbnb's fake Craigslist posts for its hosts.
- Operations: you may need real humans for checking output, such as an account manager.
- Exit angle: he says Upwork or Fiverr would probably acquire a working version. He notes Upwork's stock and Fiverr's stock are down heavily (Fiverr from about $320 to about $25 in his words) because of AI fears over low-level repetitive tasks.

chunks.heading: Humanize AI: replace a human service with AI, keep the familiar form
chunks.text:
- Principle: to get products adopted, make AI feel like the real-world experience people already know, not "Tech based." He compares it to the early iPhone, where notes looked like notes.
- Headshot Pro example: instead of scheduling a photo shoot, driving there and paying around $300, customers take 15 selfies and two hours later get photos. "The AI is literally the photographer." The experience matches a photo shoot even though no human is involved.
- Branding: he would sell it as the old service, don't foreground AI, and make it about 10x cheaper.
- Method for finding ideas: call practitioners such as your dentist, auto mechanic or barber and ask what is repetitive and hated. Danny says there is little competition because these niches are boring and programmers don't know them, so whoever learns the market and can do marketing wins it.
- Case study he cites: medical scribes. A person listens in and takes notes; Whisper plus an LLM can transcribe and summarize. He says that job is likely automated within five years. A doctor's tool called Autoscribe (Mew2 Health, Toronto) had almost no competing search results.
- Spin-offs: nurses, dentists, and veterinarians. A friend built AI note-taking for veterinarians with no competition; niche users prefer a tool built for them over a broad consumer app.
- Timing: he says SaaS is already eating the world and this niche approach will be saturated in about five to ten years, so move fast.

chunks.heading: AI-run marketing agency with productized services
chunks.text:
- Danny sold his first startup to Jasper (an AI copywriting generator).
- Idea: a marketing agency run almost entirely by AI. He owns the domain headline99, intended as a $99 landing page headline service.
- Flow: the customer fills in a questionnaire about their company; several LLMs summarize it and produce 5-10 headline ideas; a human in the loop picks the final three and you deliver the best-working headline.
- Reasoning: everyone uses software and SaaS now, but users don't know the craft, so you productize the extra layer on top. He sees broad opportunity in unbundling the marketing agency into autonomous SaaS-like services, potentially scaling with very few people.
- He says he likes the domain so much he is tempted to keep working on it, and notes projects with "head" in the name (Headshot Pro, headline99) have been successful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny explains how he ships fast AI mini products (This Model Does Not Exist, ProfilePicture.AI, Tattoos.AI) and uses them as marketing for his main product. He covers why he sold Headlime instead of scaling a team, why bigger competitors help him, and why SEO plus tools, not blog posts, is the durable way to launch.

chunks.heading: Danny's AI product-studio model: ship fast, hand off, stay small
chunks.text:
- Danny builds many small AI products instead of one big company. His stated goal is "100 AI products doing the same amount of revenue" in about 10 years, each ideally 100% automated.
- Target shape for a product: SEO traffic comes in, it earns "five six figures a month", and the only human work is live chat (his wife handles it).
- He starts products and gets bored after about three months. He says he can hyper-focus on something that interests him for a month, ship it, then lose interest. He builds around that weakness instead of fighting it.
- Division of labor: he hired an operations person (content creation, live chat) and a developer friend two weeks before this interview. Danny builds and launches new ideas. The developer builds out the "more boring features" once Danny gets bored.
- He prefers a small trusted team over managing people: "I don't want to manage the whole [...] team." Both hires are people who know what to do without being managed.
- He frames this as a deliberate choice. He could have scaled to millions of customers, but that means a big support load and a big team.
- Following curiosity is the strategy. He only works well on things that really interest him.

chunks.heading: Selling Headlime and choosing not to be a CEO
chunks.text:
- Danny built Headlime, an AI copywriting tool (blogs, emails, Facebook and Twitter ads), one of the first products built on GPT-3. He has a screenshot from OpenAI saying he was the first developer to go live with such a product, in December 2020.
- It grew fast: revenue doubled every two to three weeks, and it made a lot of revenue within three months.
- Competition arrived (he compares it to Jasper). He had talks with Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia and an acquisition offer that would have been "life-changing" money.
- He weighed three paths for one to two weeks, talking to friends, parents and his wife:
  - take funding and hire about 50 developers, becoming a CEO
  - bootstrap it
  - sell
- He decided it wouldn't be his life to "work 80 hours, manage people" and that it wouldn't make him happy, so he sold.
- His view: CEO roles are romanticized. If you're a maker, being "the boss" isn't fun. He says to work out why you're an entrepreneur and what you want before choosing.
- The first thing he did was build a tool for himself: he built Headlime because he was bad at writing headlines. His advice is to build for your own need, since "if you're lucky" thousands of others share it, and if not you still made your own life easier.

chunks.heading: ProfilePicture.ai and why competitors help a small bootstrapper
chunks.text:
- ProfilePicture.ai: a user uploads about 20 photos, a personal AI model is trained on them, and they can then prompt any scene (e.g. Game of Thrones warrior, anime style) that looks like them. He is expanding it toward LinkedIn headshots and a "photo studio".
- He expected a hype cycle but says it has persisted past three months. He says there is a lot of search volume around it and he has thousands of customers.
- Lensa launched one month after him and reportedly made about $30 million on the app store. Danny's reaction: he got roughly 10 times more sales after Lensa launched.
- Why: Lensa's marketing created awareness of "AI avatars". Some searchers used "AI profile picture" instead and landed on his domain.
- His stance changed from Headlime days, when he panicked at funded competitors. Now: "it's great if some big shots marketing money spend their build something like me because they do the marketing for me, I'll eat the scraps."
- He doesn't need $30M in revenue because he has no employees to pay.
- Strategy: niche down. Take a specific part of a big tool that people love, don't bloat it with features to chase growth, and "then you have a reason to exist". Big players use broad terms, so a niche keyword set is where a small one can win.
- He expects Instagram or TikTok to eventually ship a built-in editor where you type what you want to see in your own face, and chose not to compete there.

chunks.heading: Mini products as a marketing channel (This Model Does Not Exist)
chunks.text:
- Danny says he is bad at ads and dislikes conventional marketing. The one thing he's good at is SEO. So he launches mini products as marketing for his main product.
- This Model Does Not Exist ("A-list"): an Instagram account of a consistent AI-generated virtual influencer. A new photo is generated every 15 minutes, visitors upvote, and top-voted photos go to Instagram. Banners every 15 photos point to his main products.
- Build time: roughly a morning or an afternoon, because he already had the upload tooling and model-training knowledge from ProfilePicture.ai.
- How he made the consistent face: grabbed many fake faces from an AI face generator (he mentions Generated.photo), picked the ones that look alike, uploaded them into his training tool, retrained, and got one person who always looks the same.
- Upvoting backfired in a small way: people upvoted broken images (two hats, bad hands), so he switched to just posting the most upvoted. He says only about 5-10% of outputs are bad.
- It brings "quite some revenue" via banners to his products and is on the back burner. Possible future: turn the tech into a tool for others to create their own influencers or characters (people have DMed him asking).
- His self-assessment: he doesn't know Instagram well and would need a partner for that side.

chunks.heading: SEO-first AI products: Tattoos.ai and the keyword-difficulty method
chunks.text:
- Tattoos.ai was his first of these products. A user types a tattoo idea (example: "a bunny with a black hat"), picks a tattoo artist's style, and gets a flash sheet. A real person got one of the generated tattoos on his leg.
- Pricing: $9 for 14 days of access. He gets about one or two sales a day.
- Programmatic SEO loop: every generated tattoo's prompt becomes a search-engine-style page, auto-created (e.g. bunny tattoo, shark tattoo, wave tattoo). Users generate content, it gets published on his site, and Google can pick it up.
- He applies the same idea to LandingFolio.com (website templates). There he had to hire a developer and designer and wait about six months to have content. With AI products, user-generated output becomes site content automatically.
- Search intent argument: informational queries (like recipes) will be disrupted by ChatGPT. Solution-seeking queries (make a profile picture, get a tattoo) still go to Google, and AI can't replace the tool itself.
- He avoids AI-written copy because he fears Google penalizes it.
- Ranking view: Google rewards pages where people stay. "You just need to make things for people that they want." Blog-style content marketing is dead; tools and products are how to rank.
- He credits backlinks as the key ingredient. He builds in public mainly for backlinks: press and social links on launch day mean he doesn't wait about six months for Google to pick a new product up.

chunks.heading: Advice for starting: find a low-difficulty keyword niche
chunks.text:
- His one-liner for beginners: go to Ahrefs.com and keep typing keywords for things you're interested in until you find a cluster with keyword difficulty under 10, meaning you should be able to reach page one of Google.
- Then build a product around that cluster, optimized so content can rank. Use no-code or code, either way.
- His reasoning: many people know how to build but not how to launch or market, and SEO is the easiest way to start.
- Build something to scratch your own itch; "everyone should launch something".
- He follows this on Twitter (@dannypostmaa) and builds all his startups in public.

chunks.heading: What failed: StockAI and the AI-quality timing lesson
chunks.text:
- Danny built StockAI, a stock photo site fully run by AI: a model trained on stock-style photos running 24/7, generating hundreds of thousands of images. He had to shut it down.
- Why it failed:
  - Quality too low. It works for profile pictures because they don't need to be perfect and can be cropped (he hides hands in pockets or under tables), but stock photography is rejected over a single flaw.
  - Competition from free sources: Unsplash has millions of free high-quality photos.
  - Conversion: it got social press and lots of visitors, but the conversion rate to a paid product was 0.004, and AI models are expensive to run.
  - Legal risk: Getty is suing the makers of the open model (trained on the 5-billion-image LAION data set). As a solo founder he didn't want to face a lawsuit, so he killed the product rather than waste six months.
- His view: Midjourney is close for artistic styles but not for realistic photos yet. He might revisit it after seeing how Getty vs. Stability AI resolves.
- He also notes that StockAI didn't get engagement when building in public: "who the [...] likes stock photography." Boring products don't get shared.
- He thinks Shutterstock, with its huge photo database, is best placed to do it well.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny explains how he picks products by searching Ahrefs for high-search, low-difficulty keywords so he never has to market, why he favors one-off B2C payments over SaaS, how he handles copycats, and why he's now hiring a remote async team at 29 to run his portfolio like a studio.

chunks.heading: Why Danny only builds products with existing search demand
chunks.text:
- Danny picks product ideas by researching keywords first. He uses Ahrefs' keyword finder to see how many people search for a term and its keyword difficulty.
- His rule of thumb: with keyword difficulty under roughly 10 to 20, "you're guaranteed to go to the front page if you have like a one or two backlinks."
- He only pursues ideas with high search volume and low competition, so he never has to do marketing: "people search for it already."
- He says all the ideas on his postcrafts.com project list came from searching Ahrefs for keywords and building a product around them.
- He would not build something nobody searches for, because then "you have to create the market," which is very hard for an indie hacker.
- If a keyword has one or two competitors, he says you can still rank third. If he isn't good at SEO, he can bid on it in AdWords if the acquisition price supports it.
- He calculates the potential up front: assume a landing page conversion rate (e.g. one percent), and estimate monthly revenue at a number-one ranking.
- He says he tells everyone on Twitter to go SEO as an indie hacker, while admitting he may be biased.
- Danny calls this demand-first idea generation: start from proven search demand, then build the product.

chunks.heading: Domain names as an SEO lever, and lease-to-own domains
chunks.text:
- Danny believes the domain name helps ranking. "Headshot Pro" in the domain tells Google to rank for "headshot pro" and "professional headshot," giving "a little bit of a boost." If you want AI stock photos, get stockai.com.
- He paid $3,000 for headshotpro.com and thinks it was worth it.
- His .io lesson: with Headlime (.io), many people typed headlime.com or headlime.co into Google and couldn't find the site. He notes that someone else (Damon from Testimonial) bought the .com, put an affiliate URL on it, and paid roughly 10 to 20 thousand dollars, which he earned back from the redirected traffic.
- He argues that competitors buying your .com can cost you customers, so buying it is worth it if you can afford to.
- Lease-to-own experiment: he wanted stockai.com, but the owner wanted about $25k to $30k. On a domain marketplace he could pay in installments (12, 24, or up to 60), at a higher commission (he estimates about 20 percent extra).
- He paid about $500 a month. If you cancel before it's paid off, the owner gets the domain back.
- He paid for three months (about $1,500), never found product-market fit, and stopped paying. He sees it as a cheap way to test whether a premium domain is worth owning.

chunks.heading: From stock photos to profile pictures to AI headshots: pivoting by conversion
chunks.text:
- Generative AI took off in September 2022 with Stable Diffusion. Danny's first idea was a stock photo website (Stock AI), but quality wasn't there, people weren't willing to pay, and he feared legal action from big stock photo companies' lawyers.
- Another builder shipped a product that turned your face into styles. Danny and his friend Peter Levels built a competing version in about 30 hours; Peter shipped without a backend and database because he knew Danny would ship faster. Danny launched Saturday morning, it "exploded on Twitter," and he says he made six figures in sales in a week because it was a highly shareable, brand-new product.
- Revenue later dropped (competition such as Lensa boosted it for a while, then it fell to "barely any revenue"). He pivoted.
- He then launched Deep Agency (AI fashion and models) and Headshot Pro at the same time. Deep Agency got a lot of press but few sales, with about a 0.3 percent conversion rate. Headshot Pro had roughly 10 times that conversion rate.
- His rule: "Impressions and clicks doesn't pay the bills." If one product converts and earns 10 times more, focus on it. He shelved the fashion product because it was harder to build and a bigger company would likely dominate that space.
- His products (Stock AI, profile picture, Headshot Pro) are described as an evolution: reuse the same technology and templates, pivoting each time.

chunks.heading: Why Danny prefers B2C one-off payments over B2B SaaS
chunks.text:
- Danny used to think B2C was bad, and still acknowledges disputes, angry customers and refunds. He is moving from software to one-off purchases.
- Headshot Pro is a one-time purchase: you upload photos and get the product back. He and his wife automated refunds and customer support. When he went to Holland for two weeks, he turned on auto-refund so any customer with an issue got money back automatically.
- His reasoning on B2B vs B2C:
  - Recurring revenue is nice, but it requires continually building features and keeping a relationship with the customer.
  - In B2C one-off, "you only have to get them once to buy," there's no need to add features, and little support or help desk, since customers don't return.
  - It scales through SEO and ads. His strength is conversion optimization: building a high-converting landing page, optimizing incoming traffic, converting, delivering, and done.
- His mantra: he doesn't build tools that rely on him always being online (like email tools). He wants products where he could be gone for a week and ignoring support wouldn't be a big deal. His wife handles support for a couple of hours a day, and the team simply lets it wait roughly 16 hours overnight.
- His working time zone (Asia, 12 hours ahead of North America) means customers sleep while he works. Early on, when Headshot Pro launched, servers went offline in the first week, so he hardened it until it auto-scales.

chunks.heading: Buying small B2C sites and funneling them into the main product
chunks.text:
- Danny's acquisition logic: he acquired a site (Hashtag AI) listed on Acquire where the conversion rate was low but SEO traffic was high.
- He reasoned that if he could make the landing page convert five times better, he'd earn back the price in about 10 months (at a price of roughly four times yearly profit). At 10 times it would be about five months.
- He copied his Headshot Pro generation onto the acquired domain. He says the conversion rate is up about six times, and he expects to earn the money back in about nine months.
- He also bought profilepicturemaker.com (a 12-year-old domain). People looking for a profile picture may want a headshot, so he put a big banner linking to Headshot Pro.
- His approach: use acquired sites and tools as acquisition channels that funnel traffic back to the main product, treating it like engineering as marketing.
- He benefits from competitors' marketing. When Remini went viral with AI headshots, his sales tripled because people Googled "AI headshots," where he ranks number one, and he converts them.

chunks.heading: Market size, competition, and why Headshot Pro could last
chunks.text:
- Danny sees about five big competitors in headshots, including one VC-funded company that copied his landing page and tried to copy his marketing agency. Profile picture tools had hundreds of competitors.
- He likes VC-backed or popular competitors because "they do marketing for me."
- His market view: a physical photo shoot costs around $300, and he offers one for about $39 with results that look good "nine out of ten" times. Portrait photography is a $5 to $10 billion worldwide market in his estimate, and he'd be happy with 1 percent of it.
- He admits a bigger competitor could always hurt him, and says that with AI "you could be obsolete next year." So he prefers to get revenue up front rather than build slowly, and move to another product if needed.

chunks.heading: Handling copycats and cloned landing pages
chunks.text:
- Danny distinguishes inspiration from copycats: he's fine with people building the same product, but not with someone copying a whole landing page, copy, branding and screenshots, because customers get confused about who the real competitor is.
- With Headlime two years earlier, copycats were constant. He spent about two months fighting them and being negative on Twitter, and people got fed up with him. That frustration motivated him to take about three months to build version two of Headlime, a bigger product, to stay ahead. Version two was eventually acquired.
- In a recent incident a rage-bait tweet cloned his product. Peter Levels advised him not to feed the troll. Danny deleted his tweets and DM'd the person, noting he could file a DMCA notice with Cloudflare and have the site taken down. The person changed the copy, which Danny considers fine competition.
- His tactics:
  - Don't engage publicly, because Twitter promotes rage bait.
  - Block competitors on Twitter to stay sane. He kept the Copy AI founder blocked for about two and a half years and only unblocked him two weeks ago.
  - Most copycats ("99 percent") don't go anywhere.
- His view on reputation: building in public means your reputation is your asset, so cloning someone destroys trust with the community.

chunks.heading: Moving from solopreneur to a small remote team
chunks.text:
- Danny posted his first job ad for a machine learning engineer. Two reasons: he is burned out on building features six months into Headshot Pro (he believes he has ADHD and hadn't built anything for three weeks), and competitors are coming, so it doesn't make sense not to invest Headshot Pro's revenue in a team.
- Headlime: he sold it about two years earlier instead of building a team, because he was afraid to hire. He had three options then (VC funding, bootstrapping with a team, selling) and chose to sell. Now with Headshot Pro the only options are to sell again or build a team.
- He argues selling would bring only about a 3x multiple because Headshot Pro has no strategic acquirers, versus 8 to 10x, so it isn't worth it yet.
- His plan: hire async contractors, ideally part-time people with other clients, in the same Asia time zone. Europe was a poor fit because his friend's 10 a.m. start meant 5 p.m. for Danny and evening questions. America is impossible.
- Style: a self-managing team with larger tasks and weekly check-ins, not constantly online, which preserves the solo-founder feel.
- He is upfront with candidates that it's his first time and tells them not to quit their job for it. He treats this as scary because shipping and killing products is easy, but shipping and killing a team affects people's salaries and families.
- To learn management, he asked on Twitter to shadow remote teams. The Gumroad founder added him to Notion, and he took notes on their processes and used them to set up his own task manager.
- The intended structure: a "Danny Postma team" or studio that can work on many products, so when something finds product-market fit, the team scales it while he keeps iterating and testing new ideas.
- His exit thinking: sitting on a beach would probably depress him, so the team lets him keep building asynchronously.

chunks.heading: Building in public as distribution
chunks.text:
- Danny says most of his Twitter followers came through Peter Levels retweeting him, plus others like John Young. He went from 15K to about 87K in a few months.
- His caution: building in public attracts other indie hackers, so it only sells if your customers are indie hackers. If your audience is elsewhere, you need a different channel. He grew from 200 to 15K followers by sharing novel technology, which drew attention. For non-novel products, it may be hard to start that way, so "better just focus on a guaranteed marketing channel" such as SEO.
- Benefits: he calls Twitter his board of directors, getting feedback on things like AdWords. He is solo "only because I can ask other people." He started years ago, and says you have to start early.
- Downsides: he is addicted to Twitter, and virality brings pain. When Deep Agency tweets reached 5 to 30 million views, he got death threats. He prefers the quieter 80K size and wouldn't want to be famous.
- Life context: he lives in Indonesia (a Bali-like setup), outsourcing cooking and cleaning, which he estimates saves about four hours a day to focus on the business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny Postma explains how he taught himself to code, scratched his own itch with a string of products, and built Headlime on GPT-3 until Jasper acquired it. He also covers where AI products win (marketing, UI, private models) and why he sold instead of raising or hiring.

chunks.heading: Building Headlime: from ebook to AI product
chunks.text:
- Danny learned to code in 2019 and started from a small idea. In 2017 he and a friend wrote an ebook with about 200 headline formulas, templates with a product name as a variable.
- Around the pandemic he turned that into a simple headline-generator tool. It was a conversion-optimization product, because headline testing is most of that work.
- After OpenAI released GPT-3 in June, he rebuilt Headlime on it. It generated headlines, Facebook ads, Google ads and landing pages.
- In January he added the feature he calls the killer one: blog generation. You type an outline and the AI writes a full blog post.
- He says he was one of the first to go live with OpenAI's API. The first non-GPT-3 version took 6 months. The GPT-3 version took about 3 months from start to finish.
- Revenue was shared publicly on Twitter: about $5K in December, $10K in January, $20K in February (about $20K a month at the sale).
- He sold a $49 lifetime deal, which he calls "totally worth it" for the earlier headline generator.

chunks.heading: Selling Headlime to Jasper for seven figures
chunks.text:
- The sale was reported as seven figures. He got two offers, both by DM on Twitter. Jasper was one of them.
- He cites "normally four times the monthly revenue" as a rule of thumb for pricing a business, but notes Headlime was skyrocketing, so it deserved more. He told Jasper to double their offer, and they agreed.
- His reasons for selling:
  - Big, well-funded startups were entering the space and he was alone.
  - He was close to burnout doing support, programming and marketing. About 200 people a day were in his customer support.
  - He didn't want VC money. He says investors expect an IPO-track path and "80 hours a week", which isn't his lifestyle.
  - He grew up in a poor family, so spending his own money to bootstrap scale felt scary.
  - Hiring in a Dutch company is risky because you can't easily fire people.
  - Cashing out gave a life-changing amount of money.
- In the deal, he asked that the Headlime website stay online. Lifetime-deal customers kept access, and some flipped their accounts for thousands of dollars.
- On a customer complaining about being "abandoned": acquisitions are how a founder gets paid after "working their asses off 16 hours a day, 7 days a week", and a $49 lifetime deal was a great price.

chunks.heading: Indie hacking, building in public and lifestyle
chunks.text:
- He sees himself in the second wave of indie hackers, after Pieter Levels and others. He started with about 200 Twitter followers and grew them by sharing wins, losses, revenue and learnings while building Headlime.
- He credits sharing progress publicly as a major marketing channel and a reason the sale was possible. He now thinks it has become normal.
- He prefers "solopreneur" or "indie-preneur" now. He compares it to indie music: no big label (VC), your own schedule, one project, no employees.
- He works about 6am to midday. In the first week of Profile Picture it was about 16 hours a day.
- He is "slowmading" in Indonesia (Bali) with a house, wife and dog. He says slowmading means 3-4 months in a place instead of hopping every few weeks.

chunks.heading: How he picks product ideas and ships
chunks.text:
- He mostly scratches his own itch, because it stays fun and he is his own first customer.
- Landingfolio: there were no landing page galleries when he started, and he collected sites he liked. It got no traffic for a year, then Google picked it up. He didn't mind because he used it himself.
- The headline generator came from his conversion-optimization work.
- He likes to dive in and build, and accepts that a month might be wasted. Headlime was his third product to work. Profile Picture AI took 11 products.
- Caveat: this approach only works if you can ship quickly.

chunks.heading: Learning to code and building AI products without coding
chunks.text:
- He says he was bad at school and only learns when something is interesting.
- He taught himself in about 6 months (4 days a week full-time, with a freelance job 2 days a week covering living costs). He learned by building Landingfolio and hitting each barrier in turn: images, file uploads, databases, servers.
- Friends in Bali pointed him to Vue.js and MongoDB, then he used free YouTube crash courses (framework, MongoDB, JavaScript). He says a curriculum might have been faster.
- He says to learn to code only if you like working with computers.
- For marketers: no-code tools (Webflow, Bubble) plus AI APIs can recreate a lot. APIs mentioned: Astria (DreamBooth), Replicate, Hugging Face, Dream Studio.
- Self-hosting is a waste of time early on because APIs are so easy. Later you want your own hosting for full control over scaling and to avoid depending on a platform. He was moving Profile Picture off the Astria API to his own hosted version.
- His view of defensibility in AI products: "marketing, a good graphical user interface, and privately trained models". He notes Headlime had about 50 direct competitors when it launched.
- He uses GitHub Copilot and says about 80% of his code is generated. He expects AI to make programmers faster rather than replace them, as in "power tools".

chunks.heading: Profile Picture AI, Stock AI and the image-AI explainer
chunks.text:
- Profile Picture AI uses Stable Diffusion (open-source text-to-image) plus DreamBooth. DreamBooth lets you retrain the model on about 20 photos of your face, so prompts can place you anywhere (Santa Claus, a Roman soldier).
- It can also be trained on objects, for example a microphone.
- Prompts are found on Lexica, a visual database of images with their prompts. Dream Studio costs about 1 cent per image.
- Stock AI (stockai.com) makes unique AI stock images. A customer with a point-of-sale system for restaurants uses it to generate food photos for Uber Eats and GrabFood listings. Conversion rates reportedly went up and no one noticed it was AI.
- Pricing at the time: $19 for a Black Friday deal, and he was working on lowering fees now that GPUs were cheaper.

chunks.heading: Opportunities and trends in AI
chunks.text:
- Niche specialization works because jack-of-all-trades models are not specialized. He predicts "highly specialized DreamBooth" products with nice interfaces, later bought by Adobe.
- Lexica's founder is training a private model on high-quality photography. He thinks a private, specialized dataset is a real moat.
- Ideas he flagged:
  - Summarizing long text, video and books. OpenAI had recently allowed long text input, and Whisper transcribes audio, so video and podcasts can be turned into text and summarized.
  - A personal daily podcast: pull top news items, transcribe and summarize them, narrate with an AI voice.
  - AI-generated video game assets sold as a library. He pointed to someone doing this, as game developers struggle with design.
- He also described automated TikTok channels that pull top Reddit posts, narrate them over game footage and post at scale, keeping only the top performers.
- Longer term, he thinks content could become fully tailored to each person.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny Postma explains how he shipped several AI products in months (HeadshotPro, ProfilePicture AI, Deep Agency), what sells, and why a lone indie hacker needs distribution, SEO and stacked custom models rather than thin wrappers on a hyped model. He also covers how to start building and what to pick.

chunks.heading: Danny's AI product portfolio and what was getting traction (early 2023)
chunks.text:
Over a few months Danny built seven AI projects:
- Profile Picture AI (a Lensa-style tool)
- Tattoos AI (an AI tattoo artist)
- Deep Agency (a virtual modeling agency and photo studio)
- "This model does not exist" (an AI-generated model named Alice)
- Meme tool (people morph themselves into memes)
- Headshot Pro (corporate headshots for individuals and teams)

He says the tools spread because they feel like "indistinguishable from magic": a user uploads a few photos and gets hundreds of profile pictures back. That makes them easy to share on Instagram and TikTok. A few months after launch, Headshot Pro's live counter showed 450,000+ headshots generated, and he said it had passed a million about two weeks after going live (he updated the counter manually).

chunks.heading: Headshot Pro: what sells and why it beat the artsy tools
chunks.text:
- Headshot Pro became his biggest success in traffic and revenue.
- Customers kept asking for LinkedIn-style photos from the artsy styles of Profile Picture AI, and he followed that demand into Headshot Pro.
- It solves real problems: people with no usable photos, and people who hate photo shoots and look awkward in them.
- Remote teams are the strongest use case. A company with staff across Asia, America and Europe cannot send one photographer around the world. Everyone uploads a photo, an AI model is trained on them, and shared styles give the whole team a consistent look.
- He expects photographers to adapt rather than disappear:
  - His best customer outputs come from people who did a very basic photo shoot on a white screen first, then trained the AI on those photos.
  - He then generates hundreds of photos of them in a park, an office or anywhere else.
  - He thinks headshot photographers may move toward producing high-quality training images and using AI as "the next Photoshop".
- His framing: "Photoshop was the post-production", and AI will become the pre-production, with real photography filling gaps AI can't cover.

chunks.heading: Unit economics of AI image generation (Feb/Mar 2023)
chunks.text:
- Training a Dreambooth model on a person's face costs about 60 cents.
- Generating each image costs a fraction of a cent. He says hundreds of thousands of photos can be generated for under $100.
- A Deep Agency-style shoot with the non-existent model "Alice" is therefore very cheap.
- His main demand there came from mom-and-pop clothing brands that could never afford models for web shop photos. He sees the tool as democratizing for the low end of small business.
- Profile Picture AI pricing:
  - It started fairly expensive.
  - He kept lowering the price until it was "almost around cost price", about $5 per set.
  - Lensa, which he says did about $40M, "basically killed the whole market" after it went live.

chunks.heading: The Deep Agency viral launch and the lesson of shipping before the product is ready
chunks.text:
- He posted a tweet about Deep Agency before the product was ready. It went viral (one tweet reached about 2M people, and he cites about 30 million views overall).
- He had to ship something within 24 hours because no website was live yet.
- He says the product is "nowhere close" to what the tweet implied and that other tools do the job better.
- The underlying stack was assembled from separate research tracks:
  - Dreambooth to train an AI on a real or fake face.
  - StyleGAN to generate faces of people who don't exist.
  - Deep learning models that put a flat, top-down clothing photo onto a body.
- His view: the technology is there, and a company that understands the fashion industry has to take it further.

chunks.heading: Lesson from losing to Lensa: distribution is everything, and avoid building on hype
chunks.text:
- Profile Picture AI was essentially just Dreambooth with no moat. Lensa launched about a month after he did and made his revenue "in one hour or something like it".
- His takeaway: "Distribution is everything, marketing is everything." Indie developers like to build and skip marketing, and that is the wake-up call.
- With AI products the model gives little defensibility, so distribution matters more. Lensa hired TikTok influencers to post, and he expects someone with a bigger budget to win that way again.
- His rule: "You shouldn't build on a hype." Hype brings attention that then fades.
- His response with Headshot Pro:
  - Focus on SEO, building tools and getting backlinks so the business lasts longer than a hype cycle.
  - Pick small problems to solve.
  - Do the marketing and distribution, because "you got to sell it".
- He applies the same hype warning to novelty content such as AI-generated celebrity podcasts, where interest fades with each episode. Tools tied to a real job to be done last longer.

chunks.heading: Building a defensible product: stacking models and learning the hard parts
chunks.text:
- Headshot Pro is not a single wrapper. It is 15 different AI models stacked in sequence, each doing a separate job: training, upscaling, generating, and optimizing photo quality. Some are custom-built.
- To do this he had to learn Python and machine learning. He says deploying models used to be the hard part, but hosting startups that appeared around October 2022 made it much easier.
- He uses ChatGPT to summarize academic AI papers, since he has no academic background.
- His following on Twitter grew by showing what AI can do in a form regular people can understand: "I like to try things out, make tools out of it so it's more comprehensible for the regular Joe."

chunks.heading: How to start building AI tools and what he would build
chunks.text:
How to start:
- Use replicate.com. It hosts models such as Stable Diffusion, has simple input fields, and offers an API.
- Hook that API into a no-code tool. He mentions Zapier-style integrations that connect Stable Diffusion to email or Discord.
- He says 99% of apps you could build right now can be API wrappers with no-code tools. Coding knowledge is only needed to go deeper.

Choosing what to build:
- He would not enter image generation (Adobe and Canva do it) or chatbots (ChatGPT ships something new every week).
- Instead, pick something that annoys you and consider whether AI can speed it up.
- A looming recession means people want to save money, so ask whether the tool removes a step and saves money.
- An idea he would like to see built: a personalized daily podcast generated from Hacker News top posts and his favorite Twitter accounts, using text-to-voice and Whisper-style transcription, short enough for a morning dog walk. He thinks it is "not even that hard to build".

chunks.heading: Expected platform and market shifts
chunks.text:
- He expects social media platforms such as Instagram to integrate AI try-on within a year or so, since they already hold users' face photos and could train a model on them and place shopping-carousel clothing on the user.
- He sees AI-generated models as most useful for small brands that could not otherwise afford shoots.
- Because new models launch constantly, he says that "every time I wake up the next morning there's something new that's launched that already makes the whole technology obsolete." For that reason he builds on small problems and distribution rather than on the current state of the tech.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny Postma explains how he launched Headlime with tiered, scarcity-limited lifetime deals, listened to early customers to decide features, and grew via building in public. He also covers the downside: his easily copied product was cloned about 10 times, and he now advises caution with revenue numbers.

chunks.heading: Building in public: how Danny started and what he shares
chunks.text:
- Danny was a designer until about age 20, then trained as a conversion specialist (A/B testing, marketing psychology). After years of that he got bored of the "test something, throw it away, optimize" loop.
- In November 2019 he started teaching himself to program (HTML/CSS first, then backend). He worked "incognito" for about six months, rebuilt Landingfolio, launched it, and only then began sharing publicly (around February 2020).
- He defines building in public two ways: tweeting progress, learnings and builds on Twitter and Indie Hackers, and working in the open in person. At his Bali co-working space, Tropical Nomad, a group meets Tuesdays and Thursdays. At 10am each person pitches what they will finish, and at 4pm each gets five minutes to demo and take feedback on what people don't understand.
- He credits that in-person group for teaching him to program (database setup, integrations).
- He keeps notes of what he did well on each launch in a note tool (Mindwave) so he can reuse them on later launches.
- He wrote his Indie Hackers revenue post partly to celebrate and document the win, and partly to give back. He learned most things by lurking on Indie Hackers for two years. He saw his marketing background (landing page copy, pricing tactics) as the help the community lacked.

chunks.heading: Lifetime deals and tiered pricing for the Headlime launch
chunks.text:
- Headlime (a headline/content template tool) was priced at $9/month, with a lifetime deal as the launch offer. Landingfolio and Headlime both came from his marketing background.
- Why lifetime deals: he thinks many people are subscription-fatigued and the tool was an MVP, so asking for monthly commitment felt hard. Up-front cash also gives runway. The lifetime price was $129 against a $9/month plan, and many monthly users churn within a year.
- Use of the cash: he hired a part-time copywriter for new copy and updates, invested in tooling, and did less freelancing. He describes it as "like a small angel investment" from customers.
- Tiered, limited-quantity pricing:
  - Tier 1: $49, capped at 200 deals, with a visible counter. It sold out in 12 hours (after a Product Hunt launch), and he had to add a new tier at 3am.
  - Tier 2: $89, 200 deals, sold out in about two weeks.
  - Tier 3: $429 (stated in the talk; he mentions $129 as the lifetime price elsewhere, so the final price tiers are ambiguous beyond the first two).
- He says there is no fixed formula: raise the price and watch whether it sells. A $49 deal selling out so fast showed it was too cheap. He estimates the true value sits between $129 and $199.
- He stopped selling lifetime deals to focus on monthly subscriptions, which he calls the most important long term.
- Platforms like AppSumo and Stack Social push lifetime deal prices between $49 and $99. He thinks $49 is "completely outrageous" for lifetime access.
- Lifetime-deal communities (AppSumo Facebook groups) were a strong early-customer source. Members shared the tool across their industries, gave free marketing, and sent feature feedback.

chunks.heading: Why Headlime sold: psychology, savings and speed
chunks.text:
Danny gives three reasons for the success (about 700 sales, with roughly 10-15 refunds):
1. **Value that saves money.** Marketers always hunt for swipe files and inspiration. Over 1,000 templates (thank-you emails, survey questions, etc.) with variables for filling in company names. If it saves a marketer one hour, it has paid for itself.
2. **Scarcity (honestly applied).** He draws on Cialdini's *Influence*. With no urgency, visitors from Product Hunt, Facebook and Twitter think "I'll buy tomorrow" and forget. Limited deals with a live remaining-count push the decision.
   - He says never fake it: don't lower a price again after claiming it won't return. Customers lose trust, and earlier buyers who paid more feel tricked. His "booking.com last rooms" example: people learn to ignore fake urgency.
3. **Open, fast development.** He ships updates about twice a week (new templates, categories, requested features). Customers in the Facebook group rave about it, and he says "Danny just launches features every week."

chunks.heading: Letting customers drive the roadmap
chunks.text:
- Rule: "If three people ask me for a feature, I build it." One request is a low-signal outlier; three is near-guaranteed demand.
- About 90% of features come from customers. Early requests were for email templates, other content types and examples. Zapier integration was requested a few times and went on the backlog.
- He emails customers asking things like "I've got this idea, is it useful?" or "what content would you like?", and builds the ones that pass three requests.
- Dig into the why behind a request. A customer asked for custom variables, he built them, and she requested a refund two days later. She had been using another tool whose variables worked differently, and he never asked what she actually needed. His lesson: "customers say one thing, they probably mean something else," so ask what tool they use today and ask for examples.
- Product origin: he and a friend had written a headlines book four years earlier. The first idea was just an editable headlines tool, and customer feedback expanded it.

chunks.heading: Getting copied: what happened and how he responded
chunks.text:
- Over about two months, Headlime was copied about 10 times. He says they were not inspired copies but outright thefts: the whole landing page (built with Tailwind, so easy to copy), the headlines, the emails, the content, the videos, then sold at half price.
  - One copy launched on Stack Social before he did, so he lost that partnership.
  - Another translated his content into Portuguese and launched it in a Brazilian growth hacking Facebook group the next day.
  - Copycats posted in the same marketing channels he used, saying "same tool, half the price."
- Customers found most copies and asked in the Facebook group whether he had just bought the tool from CodeCanyon or GitHub. He spent a week of evenings defending that he wrote it. He felt it was damaging to his name, not a compliment.
- Why his product was exposed: its value is mostly copy, which is trivial to copy and paste, and the code took him about a month. He says the real work was months of writing content.
- DMCA takedowns worked, with no lawyer and about five minutes per form:
  - Use BuiltWith.com to see the copy's tech stack and hosts.
  - Search "DMCA" or "abuse" plus the provider (Amazon, Namecheap, Cloudflare) and submit the form.
  - Amazon took down about 90%; Namecheap banned domains; Cloudflare was good; Stripe was not.
- He distinguishes competitors who write their own copy and design (fine, "competition fuels me") from straight theft.
- Aftermath: he accepted it will happen, took a one-to-two-month social media break (deleted apps, a week offline), and decided to rebuild the tool to be more unique and harder to copy. He plans to share nothing until it is finished, then launch to customers first before returning to working in the open.
- Trolls on a post about the copying told him he was crying, and asked why the tool earns money if it is so easy to copy. That pushed him to step back.
- He took down his Indie Hackers revenue post because it attracted too much attention, saying money brings copies. He thought it had been too specific on his earnings.

chunks.heading: What to share and what to keep private when building in public
chunks.text:
- Danny's verdict: working in the open has been "net positive totally." He grew Twitter from about 500 to almost 5,000 followers, and most of his sales came from it.
- Benefits he lists:
  - Meeting great people (e.g., a conversion-optimization mentor who DM'd him about the tool).
  - Free ongoing marketing: when he did not tweet for a week, sales dropped drastically.
  - Opportunities such as this podcast.
  - Inspiration for others, like his own start after seeing Pieter Levels earn from a site.
- Revenue tweets gave the most engagement and roughly doubled his followers, but also attract copycats.
- Guidance when your product is easily copyable (especially copy-based products):
  - Be careful sharing revenue numbers.
  - Don't share inner knowledge that is your competitive advantage.
  - Keep sharing learnings and what you are working on.
- Products that are harder to copy (tech-heavy ones like Roam Research or Notion) can be more open.

chunks.heading: Danny's product lineup (as of October 2020)
chunks.text:
- Landingfolio: landing page inspiration.
- Headlime: quick content generation (templates for headlines, emails, surveys).
- Parity Bar: lets you offer price discounts by country; he built it in 24 hours.
- InspireFrame: a tool for quickly making website mockups.
- He was based in Bali, Indonesia (moved after backpacking from 2017), working about six days a week from his own schedule and surfing in between. He said he had no email list at the time and linked everything from Twitter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny walks through the autonomous agent system he built over six months on Claude managed agents. It runs tasks, triggers, cron automations and open-ended goal loops in isolated containers, and only pings him via an inbox when stuck. The video covers agent permission walling, template-driven dev workflows, spend caps and cost control.

chunks.heading: Agent OS: the setup and why Danny built it
chunks.text:
- Six months before this video, Danny worked in Claude Code in the terminal with his laptop open. He decided that was "quite stupid" and wanted overnight runs, cron jobs and triggers that start tasks while he is away.
- He built the first month of the system by hand with Claude Code. After that the system built itself.
- He says it now runs most of his businesses and most of his coding, and that he automated about 95% of his tasks. He does little programming manually.
- He has no name for it beyond "Agent OS".
- The system is a UI on top of Anthropic's Claude Managed Agents API and SDK. That API handles sessions, MCP connections and the Files API.
- Danny describes the loop as: set a goal (for example "ship a new landing page"), break it into tasks or hand it to the goal system, and agents work it. Tasks move through to do, doing, review and done.
- Each session runs in its own container. The container pulls the repo, mounts the file system, does the task, commits and cleans up. It is thrown away afterwards, so the next session starts clean.
- Agents message him only when they need him, through an inbox. He can go running or out with his wife and the work continues until an agent gets stuck.

chunks.heading: Agent design: one job per agent, walled-off access
chunks.text:
- Each agent has a name, title, model, prompt, skills, MCP access, file access and environment. Examples are a default agent, senior dev, plan agent, review coordinator and librarian.
- Every agent gets a shared "Agent OS foundational prompt" that explains which files, systems and MCPs it can reach. Its role prompt is layered on top.
- The plan agent has one job: turn an approved spec into a concrete implementation plan, write it to the task and finish.
- Danny's rule: "you don't want to give any access to your agent that they don't need."
- His customer support bot has the Front MCP. It has no Gmail and no GitHub repo access, so a prompt injection cannot leak code from customer support.
- The plan agent gets plan mode and the Agent OS MCP only. It has no Ahrefs and no GitHub MCP, so a leaked prompt has nothing to act on.
- Each agent has a collaboration list that controls which other agents it can spawn as subtasks.
- Environments set network access. An agent can be limited to a single host such as api.front.com. Everything else, including GitHub, is blocked at the base level even if the agent tries.
- Skills attach to agents. For example `/plan` is a plan-mode skill, and a skill can include files such as a Python script.

chunks.heading: File system, MCPs and secrets
chunks.text:
- Containers don't persist files, so Danny put Cloudflare R2 storage behind an MCP.
- Each agent gets its own folder. It can read other folders only if granted access.
- Server-side checks enforce permissions. For example, an agent can be write-only and cannot delete, because deletes must go through the MCP.
- He can open, edit, download and preview any agent file from the UI.
- Repos are registered with the GitHub repo, mount path, credential file and a personal access token.
