- Environment variables are injected into the session and stored encrypted with Google's token encryption system. He could not recall its name. He uses this to give an agent a read-only MongoDB connection, for example.

chunks.heading: Tasks and the spec-to-PR template
chunks.text:
- Tasks are a kanban board. A task can run once immediately, be scheduled, or recur (for example, summarize his inbox every Monday).
- Tasks can start from templates. His "compound engineer workflow" template for a new feature is "like a 3-hour fully managed" run.
- Each step is a follow-up task bound to a specific agent and prompt. Some steps need his approval, and the next step starts only when a task is marked done:
  1. Write a spec (needs his approval).
  2. A plan agent turns the spec into a plan.
  3. A review coordinator spawns four review agents (feasibility, scope guardian, coherence and others). They write reports, and the coordinator consolidates them into must-fix and should-fix lists.
  4. Another agent revises the plan from the review.
  5. An implementation agent writes the code.
  6. A review coordinator reviews the code.
  7. A senior dev applies the review fixes.
  8. A librarian updates an internal wiki on how the code base works.
  9. Danny reviews the deployment.
- One example task started at 3:00 p.m. and finished about 5 hours later, partly because he forgot to answer a question. He wakes up to a PR.
- He says it works 99% of the time because end-to-end testing is built in.

chunks.heading: Inbox, mobile access and live visibility
chunks.text:
- The inbox is an MCP that agents write to. His replies go back to the agent. Agents can wait for a reply, ask open-ended questions, or send multiple-choice questions with tabs and radio buttons.
- The app is mobile responsive and a progressive web app. He gets push notifications at the gym when an agent needs help or finishes.
- He can open any session as a live stream and see which tools are being called. At the time, his game's farming feature was being implemented that way.

chunks.heading: Triggers and automations in production
chunks.text:
- Triggers are webhook-started jobs. Customer support chat messages at Hedgehog Pro fire a webhook. An agent with access to customer support reads the chat and assigns it to a support rep or an account executive. That trigger had fired 600 times.
- A bug-report trigger fires when support submits a bug in the back end. A diagnostic agent has access to the repo and the support chat and writes a report on the cause. If he approves the finding, the system runs plan, plan review, fix and end-to-end testing. He only reviews and merges, so he no longer does big bug fixes by hand.
- Automations are cron-style schedules. Example: a bot that creates the company's LinkedIn content on the first of the month, automated end to end.

chunks.heading: Goals: open-ended work with a definition of done
chunks.text:
- Tasks suit structured work. Goals suit open-ended implementation and are what people now call a "gauntlet loop".
- A goal runs against a definition of done. He writes it, or feeds in a spec and the system writes the success criteria for him to approve. The loop continues until every box is checked.
- An orchestrator spawns a session, then checks the progress logs, the definition of done and what has been implemented. It decides the next step. It might spawn a senior dev to implement a feature or a plan agent to write a plan.
- Agents share an inbox and a file system and keep a progress log.
- Guardrails on every goal:
  - A spend cap. He ran one goal without a cap one night and it "ran up to $1,000".
  - A maximum run time.
  - A stuck limit: after 19 identical iterations the orchestrator stops the run.
- His daily routine: write a spec in the morning, throw it into the goal system, approve the definition of done, and let it run 5 to 6 hours. At the end of the day he reviews and merges the PR, then starts again.
- He says his whole video game is being developed by this system.

chunks.heading: Cost and runners
chunks.text:
- Running everything on Claude Managed Agents got expensive. He was spending about $500 a day.
- He added local runners: a $10 Hetzner VM running Claude with dangerously-skip-permissions and Grok in yolo mode. Work goes to the cloud when it is busy and otherwise runs locally. A goal can be pinned to local runners only.
- He assigns models by role. Planners stay on Fable, and workers run on Grok ("Grok 4.6 is really fast"). Model and runner are set per agent.

chunks.heading: Config as code and the CLI
chunks.text:
- Every project has an AgentOS folder that mirrors the online setup. Agents, skills and templates are all YAML files, and an agent's file holds its model, skills, MCP connections, repo and prompt.
- A CLI can push and pull these files and create projects.
- He brainstorms with Claude locally. Then he tells the CLI to create a goal or session in Agent OS with all the details. It creates the task and picks the agents.
- He builds the loop templates by having Claude Code write the YAML steps, which saves the manual work. Templates use variables such as the branch name.
- He offered to open-source his agents, skills and prompts on GitHub if viewers ask in the comments.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny explains a free AI skill that fixes sloppy, generic AI landing pages. It scans your brand once, explores several hero or section designs with trade-offs, lets you combine options, then implements the winner. He runs it section by section because AI can't hold a whole page in context.

chunks.heading: Why AI landing pages look like slop, and the skill Danny built to fix it
chunks.text: Danny was frustrated that, however good AI has become, it still outputs generic, uncreative, inconsistent landing pages that "look like AI." While working on a new landing page for one of his companies, he built a skill to push AI toward higher quality, more creative, more visually pleasing designs. He published it free at danny.md. His framing: one skill turns an "AI slop generator" landing page into something people would "love to look at, would love to use."

chunks.heading: How the explore-design skill works
chunks.text:
- **Brand scan (runs once).** When he asks the AI to explore directions for a section such as the hero, the skill first scans the project's color system, typography and overall design style.
- **Component-level exploration.** It then looks at the elements in the section being designed and explores several distinct, unique design directions that could suit the project.
- **Runtime and model.** The exploration normally takes 5 to 10 minutes. Danny "highly recommend[s] using Fable" for this step.
- **Output.** When finished, it opens the browser with a comparison of options and their trade-offs.
- **Invocation.** He types `/explore design` and points it at the section (for example, the hero).

chunks.heading: Reviewing options and locking one in
chunks.text:
- The skill returns four options for a section (e.g. a home page hero). Each comes with its own trade-offs, the risk, and what happens if you pick it, so it helps him decide direction rather than just dumping mockups.
- The input was an undesigned, unstyled section; the output was four styled alternatives.
- Danny liked one option for its clear call to action ("where to drop your photo") but felt it lacked a visual showing what the site actually does. He told the skill to combine it with option A into a new "option E": a drop zone plus the earlier visual. The result had a clear place to start the generator and visuals on the right side. He called it "amazing."
- Tactic: you can mix and merge options by instruction rather than accepting only what is generated.

chunks.heading: From chosen design to implemented page
chunks.text:
- After he says "lock in E," the skill extracts the design from the HTML file it created.
- It checks whether all requirements for photos and visuals are present. If something is missing, it asks whether to pick a certain asset or limit the design to a certain area.
- Then it implements the design into the real landing page.

chunks.heading: Work section by section, not the whole page
chunks.text:
- Danny runs the process for every section of the landing page (hero, before/after, how the PFP maker works, and so on).
- His reason: the AI does not have the context to hold a whole landing page, or a full-page screenshot, at once. Designing everything in one go produces worse results.
- His workflow per section: run explore, get options, choose one, refine it a little, then move on to the next section.

chunks.heading: Not just for landing pages
chunks.text:
- Danny says the skill works for "basically everything," not only landing pages.
- Example: the editor in his product. Its output was "absolute undesigned slop." After running the skill and getting inspiration, it produced a design where he could upload a photo, and it "works much much better."

chunks.heading: Installing the skill
chunks.text:
- It is free on Danny's site: go to danny.md and open the explore design file, which documents how it works.
- Pick your AI harness (his is Claude Code), copy the install line and paste it into your terminal. It unpacks the archive and places the skill in your skills folder.
- Restart the AI session, type `/explore design`, and it starts running.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny explains how he turned an old headline-formulas book into a tool, launched with a lifetime deal, then pivoted to GPT-3 and grew from $1K to $20K MRR in public before selling to Jarvis.ai. Lessons on building for yourself, shipping fast, and building in public.

chunks.heading: How Danny validated and built Headlime into a $1M+ exit in 8 months
chunks.text:
- Danny started Headlime in 2020 during lockdown by writing down ideas that were "easy to build and validate before wasting years on them."
- He picked the idea that turned an asset he already owned into a tool. Three years earlier, he and a friend wrote a book called Headline Formulas, which sold a few hundred copies.
- He chose to turn the book into a tool for two reasons: books are worth less than tools, and he already had all the content, so building was easy.
- Version one took one month. It was a simple "content spinner" with 200 headline formulas that users customized by filling in variables, outputting 200 customized headlines.
- The timeline ran from launch (about October 2020), through version 2 in December 2020 at $1K MRR, to $20K MRR in February 2021 and acquisition by Jarvis.ai in March 2021.
- He says: "Make something you'd like to use yourself. Even if no one buys it, it's still worth something to you. Furthermore, you are the most knowledgeable customer and know exactly what you want."
- Landingfolio, his earlier design gallery, started the same way. He couldn't come up with solid landing page ideas for clients as a freelance conversion optimization specialist, so he built the tool he needed.

chunks.heading: The lifetime-deal launch that made $60,000 in the first few weeks
chunks.text:
- The version one launch did over $60,000 in sales in the first few weeks, and it was his first successful product launch.
- Most of it came from a limited deal that gave customers access for a one-time fee instead of a subscription.
- Before Headlime, he ran Inspireframe, launched in June 2020. There he tried many launch techniques, documented them, and reused them all for Headlime.
- The launch lesson he draws is to put the product in front of customers early rather than working for a year without launching.

chunks.heading: Listening to customers and shipping fast after launch
chunks.text:
- Customers' vision of the product was "beyond my wildest ideas." They wanted more than headline templates: emails, Facebook headlines, Google Ads and other content types.
- He went on a "shipping spree," launching new features and content and updating the tool to match what users asked for.
- His rule: "Ship often and quickly. The only way to see if there is demand for your product is by putting it in front of customers."
- He advises putting out a minimum viable product: "If it has potential, your customers will give you valuable feedback on how to shape it further."

chunks.heading: Betting on GPT-3 and rebuilding as Headlime v2
chunks.text:
- About two months after Headlime launched, OpenAI released GPT-3, a neural network that writes content.
- He messaged the CTO of OpenAI to get access and got it.
- He quickly saw the AI was very good at producing marketing copy. With proper training, you could explain your business and it would output near-perfect copy for ads, blogs and websites.
- His read was that content spinners were done and AI-generated content was the future, so he went all in.
- He went "off the grid" for five months and used all his working hours and free time to build version 2, an AI-powered copy generator.
- Version 2 launched in December 2020. Revenue went from $1K MRR at the start of December to $20K MRR in February 2021, roughly doubling every few weeks.
- The rebuild also answered copycats. He says he outran them by being "innovative enough" with version 2.

chunks.heading: Growth through building in public on Twitter
chunks.text:
- Most growth was organic. Danny is part of the "build in public" group on Twitter that shares learnings, numbers and progress.
- While building v2, he dropped occasional teasers on Twitter showing how powerful the new tool was, so the December launch arrived with hype already built.
- Many of his tweets went viral, which created a flywheel. Bigger accounts saw them on their timelines and learned about Headlime, and that led to a TechCrunch feature (March 2021).
- His case for building in public: "A product won't market itself," and sharing what you're working on is an easy way to market it.
- On copycats: "Yes, others might copy you, but is your product actually good if no one wants to copy it?"
- Pricing was $29 a month, rising to $59. He frames it as a no-brainer for a tool that does all your copywriting, because copywriting is hard and creative ideas are harder.

chunks.heading: Why he sold: solo-founder overload and the exit decision
chunks.text:
- He ran Headlime alone. He spent hours a day on customer support, had to ship features fast as many companies cloned Headlime's success, and did all the marketing at once.
- He was too overwhelmed to train or hire anyone.
- He saw three options: take venture funding and work 80 hours a week for years, bootstrap and risk being overtaken by funded competitors, or sell.
- In February 2021 he got two acquisition offers from two prominent tech startups. He accepted one, and Jarvis.ai acquired Headlime in March 2021 for a 7-figure sum.
- He calls it the right decision: "I like to start things, not manage things."
- He describes the stress of running a high-growth solo business: churn messages in the morning could ruin his day, and a competitor raising funding made him fear his days were numbered. Selling calmed his mind.

chunks.heading: Handling copycats, negativity and imposter syndrome
chunks.text:
- Entrepreneurs plagiarized Headlime, stealing the code and content and relaunching it under another name. This made him cynical at first.
- His conclusion is that a successful product will get copied, and the answer is to work harder to stay more innovative than the copycats. Launching v2 was how he did it.
- Being in the spotlight brought negative comments from customers and competitors trying to sabotage him.
- A supportive group of fellow entrepreneurs cheered him up and helped with imposter syndrome.

chunks.heading: Tools and stack he used
chunks.text:
- Notion for note-taking and product management.
- Twitter for marketing and publishing progress.
- Heroku to host products.
- Backend: NodeJS, MongoDB and Digital Ocean.
- Frontend: Heroku and Nuxt.
- He names *Influence* as the book that taught him marketing and *Obviously Awesome* as the one for product positioning.
- He follows podcasts including Indie Hackers, My First Million and How I Build This.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny Postma traces his path from Landingfolio and Headlime to HeadshotPro, showing how he pivoted fast when the market spoke. He covers shipping in 30 hours, differentiating on quality and focus, and overcoming his fear of hiring.

chunks.heading: From Landingfolio to Headlime: building small products first
chunks.text:
- Danny started Landingfolio in 2015 at age 21, while working as a freelance Conversion Optimization Specialist. He struggled to produce effective landing page designs for clients, so he built a gallery of the best landing page designs on the internet as a side project.
- He did not know how to program at the time and built it on WordPress, which he found "much easier than I expected."
- The site still exists and gets thousands of visitors, but it is hard to monetize, so he moved on to other projects.
- Headlime started as a non-AI tool. While working on Landingfolio he wrote an interactive book of 200 headlines where users could input variables to customize the headline to their use case. He realised this would work better as software, and turned it into a simple copy spinner that did the replacing for you.

chunks.heading: Getting into AI early with GPT-3
chunks.text:
- A friend introduced Danny to GPT-3 while he was working on Headlime. He reached out directly to Greg Brockman, then CTO of OpenAI, to request access, and got in as part of the first batch of users.
- He experimented with letting GPT-3 write the templates for Headlime and was "astounded by its ability to generate copy". That turned Headlime into an AI copywriting tool.
- He credits some luck: he was already building a copywriting tool when a copywriting AI arrived. He was one of the first people to implement GPT-3 in a production environment, alongside Copy.AI and a few other tools.
- The pattern: he was already close to a problem space, so a new technology slotted straight into an existing product.

chunks.heading: Pivoting fast: from Stock AI to ProfilePicture.AI to HeadshotPro
chunks.text:
- Stable Diffusion launched in September 2022. Danny first built "Stock AI", a stock photo site, but quality fell short and he worried about legal action from image-rights owners like Getty Images, so he pivoted.
- He saw Dreambooth launching an AI service that could transform faces and realised he was building something similar. He launched his product within 30 hours, beating a competitor to market.
- ProfilePicture.AI "exploded on Twitter" and generated significant sales in its first week. He calls it a highly shareable product, and he also ranked well on Google for profile picture searches.
- When excitement faded and sales dropped, he pivoted again. He teamed up with David, a developer friend, and built a Python model that could manipulate photos into different poses, which pointed him at AI headshots.
- He launched Deep Agency and HeadshotPro at the same time. Deep Agency got a lot of press but no sales. HeadshotPro was "an instant hit", so he focused on it.
- His takeaway: "staying flexible and reacting to what the market is telling you." Press attention is not demand; sales are.

chunks.heading: Differentiating HeadshotPro: quality and a single focus
chunks.text:
- **Photo quality is the primary differentiator.** Danny says competitors mostly rely on open-source models (Stable Diffusion with DreamBooth), which "simply aren't good enough for realistic photo generations."
- HeadshotPro runs a large backend pipeline, deploying dozens of extra open-source and custom models to, in his words, "10x the output quality". The team had worked on its own custom models for a full year as of early 2024.
- Models in the pipeline include LLaVa, used to filter bad user uploads and remove NSFW generations, and Codeformer, which removes AI artifacts from faces and makes them more realistic.
- His quality bet: if the model improves 1% each day, headshots can become indistinguishable from real photos within a year, widening the gap over less serious competitors.
- **Focus exclusively on professional headshots.** Many competitors expand horizontally into dating photos, cute avatars and a full photo studio. Danny sees those detours as a distraction and says his sole focus is the highest quality professional AI headshots.

chunks.heading: Product improvements on the roadmap
chunks.text:
- Daily iteration on headshot quality is the main lever.
- Clothing generation: he expected "virtual try on" services to draw more interest in 2024 and wanted to use that tech for corporate customers, who often ask for matching suits across employees' headshots.
- User experience: the product requires 15-17 input photos, which he says has been "the magic number" for maximizing quality. The team is exploring ways to make upload easier without losing quality.

chunks.heading: Moving from solopreneur to building a team
chunks.text:
- Danny's early fear of hiring pushed him to automate as much as he could himself, especially in pre-AI times.
- As HeadshotPro grew he saw three options: sell the business, stay a solopreneur, or build a team. He chose the team, despite it being scary, because he wanted to scale.
- He describes it as an identity shift: he had to admit he didn't have all the answers, and the goal changed from running a business to leading people to build something together.
- Tactics he used:
  - Told candidates from the first interview that he was inexperienced at managing people and that there might be bumps.
  - Started with contractors and part-time people who already had other clients, as a safety net while he learned team management.
- Looking back, he says he "should have started a team way earlier." His small team does things he "could have never ever done myself," and sharing wins makes the work less lonely and more fun.

chunks.heading: Selling off side projects to focus
chunks.text:
- Danny has built many small AI products: Tattoos AI (tattoo generator), Alice (an AI social media experiment), Profile Picture AI, Deep Agency (virtual AI-generated models) and Meme Morph.
- Since HeadshotPro took off, these got little attention. He was in the process of selling most of them to focus fully on HeadshotPro.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Danny Postma explains how he sold Headlime for seven figures, made $50K in two weeks with Profile Picture AI, and what he learned about clones, lifetime deals, domains, landing pages and building on API infrastructure. Core lessons: ship in public, differentiate on marketing and UI, validate with one-time payments, and use existing infrastructure for speed.

chunks.heading: Landing pages: Danny's repeatable conversion template
chunks.text:
- Danny has used the same hero for 5 to 10 years: picture on the right, a three-point checklist, title, subtitle, a really good button, and only one call to action. He calls it "CRO 101".
- The page works through the checklist from Robert Cialdini's *Influence*: social proof (people already using it), authority (logos) and scarcity. He says someone who doesn't know marketing can learn it from that book.
- Scarcity: every time he removed the scarcity banner on profile picture AI, conversion dropped. He never lies about it, so he keeps finding new honest offers. A "buy one, get one free" banner became "40 bonus photos", and he says he won't bring either back.
- He shows real examples on the page and lists only the photos and headers that converted best.
- Copy is the most common mistake he sees. Founders know how to explain their product but not how to market it.
  - His advice: use an AI copywriter, describe what the product does, and put the output on the page.
  - "You don't even need a design": a blank page with a photo, title, subtitle and call to action is enough.
  - "People buy the template, make it fancy, but the copywriting is wrong." If visitors don't understand it in 500 milliseconds, they're gone. "You can't polish a turd."
- There are three ways to pitch: tell, have others tell (testimonials), or show. He says the best page does all three.
- Keep it simple: show a problem, present the solution, and say why you are the right person to deliver it. No "sketchy" fancy titles.
- A hyper-focused product has a clear "why" that can be explained in a second. That "why" keeps motivation high, which broader products like Intercom lose.
- He learned landing page design 10 to 13 years ago from the site One Page Love.

chunks.heading: Pricing: lifetime deals first, subscriptions later
chunks.text:
- For long-term revenue he says MRR wins, because money keeps coming in without constant marketing if churn is low.
- To validate an idea he prefers a one-time payment. He has been switching many products to one-time pricing "because it's so much easier to get sales".
- He launched StockAI with a subscription and got about ten subscribers. A one-time payment let people try it faster.
- Headlime launched as a lifetime deal, and he added subscriptions later. The sequence is:
  - Get people into the product and talking about it.
  - Add the features they actually want.
  - Then layer a subscription on top. "An expensive subscription is not going to work" at the start.
- Early lifetime buyers are "your core fans, your actual investors". They took the risk, and he thinks they deserve to be rewarded for life.
- Headlime's lifetime plan cost $49 for roughly five years of a GPT-3 copywriter, about $1 a month. When he sold the company he negotiated that Headlime stays online and lifetime holders keep their plan. It was still online two years later.
- Some people called him a sellout anyway. He says the deal was good and he added many features.
- He found a black market for lifetime deals. People resold $49 plans for thousands of dollars on Facebook Marketplace, and some bought 20 to 30 as investments.
- He learned about it when a Twitter follower with about 300 followers posted Headlime in a lifetime-deal Facebook group before launch. Danny had just read *Influence* and was applying lifetime deals and scarcity, and he didn't yet know what AppSumo was.
- Resellers sell old Zapier-style lifetime deals to big companies for around $20,000.

chunks.heading: Competing on AI products, clones and avatar hype
chunks.text:
- Profile picture AI made $50,000 in its first two weeks. Margins collapsed when Lensa priced at $2.99, below cost, as a loss leader. Danny calls them "the Amazon of AI". He still makes a few dozen sales a day.
- His view is that avatars will be commoditized and the trend will fade after Christmas, so "you've got to milk it now". Then he builds a product around what people actually want.
- His long-term edge is SEO. He got lucky choosing the "profile picture" name because people search for it. After the hype he plans to focus on SEO and be first in that market.
- Mistake he names: he didn't build a mobile app in week one. He should have hired someone, because search interest moved to the App Store and he missed those downloads. He tried learning React Native in about ten days, then dropped it once the hype faded.
- When everyone uses the same models (Jasper, Copy.ai and others use the same tech), the only differentiators are marketing and a crisp UI. "If your UI sucks, why would anyone use your tool?"
- Lensa won on distribution: an existing app with millions of users, push notifications, and Apple handling payments.
- Lensa also grew by hiring 30 to 40 influencers in Indonesia who all posted on Instagram.
- Cloning is a positive: Headlime clones forced him to build Headlime 2.0. Without them he says he might have "chilled" and not built the next product.
- Ship in public. Pieter Levels and he got cloned 100 times, but without public shipping nobody would know the products. "No one is going to copy a bad product." If you're too scared of clones you never take off, and clones come once you succeed anyway.
- He now keeps quiet about the "secret sauce": AI tricks and SEO tactics. He still shares revenue because it drives engagement.
- You can only know what to build by listening to customers. Headlime started as a headline generator. After launch customers asked for emails and Facebook ads, and someone suggested GPT-3. "You cannot build it in secret for a year."

chunks.heading: Build stack: use infrastructure to move fast
chunks.text:
- Stack for recent products: Next.js, MongoDB, hosted on Heroku. He says the stack "doesn't matter at all".
- He tried self-hosting and called it "hell". It worked, but scaling was a problem because it ran single-threaded.
- AI providers he named: Replicate (you can request a model from GitHub and they upload it), Hugging Face, and a hosted Dreambooth service for the DreamBooth products.
  - Risk: they set the prices and can change them. "If they're out then you're out."
  - Still, without them he wouldn't have earned the profile picture money.
- Rule: validate first, then build your own stuff. "Use infrastructure. It creates speed, and speed is your validation and your actual low investment."
- "You pay five times more for the API, but you save 2 to 3 weeks of your time while someone else could have launched. That time is already worth all the money."
- Web3 experience: he built a smart contract project and quit after 4 to 5 months. Contracts can't be updated, so one bug could lose users' money. A single contract took three months with security work. That pace didn't suit someone who ships in a day and builds an app in 30 days.

chunks.heading: Domains: .com, leasing and brand names
chunks.text:
- Stock AI domain: he leases stock.ai (spoken as "stock AI") at $300 a month on a 60-month installment plan, about $18,000 total against a $20,000 asking price. He owns it after 60 payments.
  - If the idea fails he cancels anytime and loses only what he paid. He paid $600 for the first two months.
  - He calls it genius for founders: a good brand name for a few hundred dollars if validation fails.
- He bought headlime.com for $3,000 after launching on headlime.io. At the time that was about 10% of what he'd earned. His top Google query was "headlime com", because people didn't know the domain and typed .com.
- He thinks the .com helps many companies, since someone could take it and build a competitor. He doesn't know if it affected the Jasper acquisition.
- Advice: you can start with .io and upgrade to .com later. He cites a founder who paid $30,000 for the .com of a testimonials company and recouped it through an affiliate link on mistyped traffic.
- He says he has a "brilliant" .com idea for about $3,000 as a follow-up and will buy it once he has a company to put on it. He declined to name it.
- Naming: people heard "Headlime" on podcasts and it stuck. "Branding is everything."

chunks.heading: Exit, money and personal finance
chunks.text:
- He sold Headlime to Jasper for a seven-figure sum. The sale took three weeks, he worked there one week, and it closed after four weeks. He was burned out, so he didn't push hard. He says he "could maybe have gotten double", but isn't complaining. There is a non-compete until 2024.
- Lessons:
  - Hire a lawyer to check the contract and add solid clauses (he did).
  - Consult a tax advisor before selling, not after.
  - Talk to people who've sold before negotiating.
- He calls himself financially independent: "you don't have to do things you don't like". Before the sale he made short-term decisions out of stress. Now he focuses on long-term things and new learning.
- He is conservative: he bought a laptop and a house and invested the rest. He treats it as retirement money paying dividends, and new startups are for a nicer life now (for example, flying home more often).
- He found startup motivation from building things he uses himself: "you made a product for yourself", and thousands of others liked what he liked.

chunks.heading: Distribution, markets and team
chunks.text:
- His wife ran the Indonesian push for profile picture AI. She contacted influencers, who posted on Instagram (2 and 3 million followers), and it drove lots of traffic from Indonesia. The catch: many people there don't have credit cards and Stripe doesn't cover local payments, so conversion was limited to people with PayPal.
- Local payment methods are super apps and QR codes. He thinks an Indonesian-language version with local payments is a golden opportunity (Indonesia has about 500 million people, most not English speakers), though payments are hard to set up.
- He dislikes partnerships ("90% big mouth, big words"). He prefers working with translators or localizers.
- Working with his wife: she is a realist and he is a dreamer. After she woke him at 6 a.m. with customer questions, he set ground rules (no live chat questions after 5 p.m., no work before 7:30). Three weeks in it was working well.
- Idea he said he couldn't build earlier for lack of tech: a spoken morning digest of top Hacker News and Product Hunt stories. He also sees an opportunity in AI dubbing of creators' videos (like MrBeast's manual multi-language voice actors) into other languages.

chunks.heading: AI outlook and ethics
chunks.text:
